title: Silent letters, liaison and élision
goal: Know which final letters are silent, link words with liaison, and shorten je, le, la, de and ne before a vowel.

items.en: élision: je, le, la, de, ne, ce lose their vowel before a vowel or silent h

drills.explain: ami starts with a vowel, so le becomes l'.
je + ai → j'ai. The apostrophe is required.
The h of hôtel is silent, so the word really starts with a vowel: l'hôtel.

items.en: liaison: a silent final consonant is pronounced before a vowel

drills.prompt: In “vous êtes”, the s of vous sounds like…
drills.explain: In liaison, s and x sound like z: vou-z‿êtes.

drills.prompt: Where do you hear a z sound?
drills.explain: Liaison only happens before a vowel sound: lé-z‿amis. Before a consonant, the s stays silent.
Never make a liaison after et (and): et | un thé.

items.note: ami and amie sound the same. Un‿ami: liaison with n.
Silent h, and the final l is pronounced.

blocks.body: Listen for the places where two words **flow into one**: [[mes amis]] sounds like “mé-z‿amis”, [[vous êtes]] like “vou-z‿êtes”. And look at the little apostrophes: [[d'où]], [[j'habite]], [[d'accord]].

steps.title: Three rules that change how French sounds

blocks.title: 1. Most final consonants are silent
blocks.body:
At the end of a word, **s, t, d, x, z, p** are usually **not pronounced**: [[vous]], [[salut]], [[tout]], [[Paris]], [[deux]] (two). A final **-e** is silent too: [[madame]], [[rue]], [[école]].

This is why the plural **-s** is silent: [[le café]] and [[les cafés]] end with the same sound. You hear the plural in the little word in front: **le** vs **les**.

blocks.title: The CaReFuL rule
blocks.body:
Four final consonants are **often pronounced**: **C, R, F, L**, as in the English word *careful*.

- **c**: [[avec]] (with), [[parc]] (park)
- **r**: [[bonjour]], [[pour]] (for), [[bonsoir]]
- **f**: [[chef]] (boss, chef), [[neuf]] (nine)
- **l**: [[il]] (he), [[hôtel]], [[Noël]]

**Big exception:** the ending **-er** usually sounds like **é**, with a silent r: [[parler]] (to speak), [[premier]] (first). Also [[monsieur]]: the r is silent.

blocks.title: 2. Liaison: a silent letter wakes up
blocks.body:
When a word ending in a silent consonant is followed by a word starting with a **vowel sound** (or a silent h), the consonant is pronounced and **jumps onto the next word**. This is called **liaison**.

- **s, x → z**: [[les amis]] (“lé-z‿amis”), [[vous êtes]], [[nous avons]], [[deux enfants]]
- **n → n**: [[un ami]] (“un-n‿ami”), [[on a]] (we have)
- **t → t**: [[c'est un ami]] (“c'est-t‿un”), [[Comment allez-vous ?]]

Liaison is **required** inside tight groups: little word + noun ([[les amis]], [[un ami]]) and pronoun + verb ([[nous avons]], [[vous êtes]], [[ils ont]]). **Never after et** (and): [[un café et | un thé]]. After [[c'est]] it is very common but not compulsory.

blocks.title: 3. Élision: the apostrophe
blocks.body:
Some very short words **drop their vowel** before a word starting with a vowel or a silent h. The vowel is replaced by an **apostrophe**, and the two words are said as one.

- **je → j'**: [[j'ai]] (I have), [[j'habite]] (I live)
- **le, la → l'**: [[l'ami]], [[l'école]], [[l'hôtel]]
- **de → d'**: [[d'accord]] (OK), [[d'Ottawa]] (from Ottawa), [[d'où]] (from where)
- **ne → n'**: [[Ce n'est pas l'hôtel.]] (It's not the hotel.)
- also **ce → c'**: [[c'est]] (it is), and **si → s'** before *il*: [[s'il vous plaît]]!

Unlike English *I'm* or *don't*, élision is **not optional**: [[je ai]] is always wrong, in speech and in writing.

head: Before a consonant
Before a vowel or silent h
English

blocks.body:
- **Je ai / le ami / la école:** always shorten: [[j'ai]], [[l'ami]], [[l'école]]. The app will flag this mistake.
- **Pronouncing the plural s:** [[les cafés]] ends like [[café]]. Don't say “ca-fez”.
- **Liaison after et:** say [[et | un thé]], never “é-t‿un”.
- **A few h's block élision and liaison** (the “h aspiré”). You say [[le hockey]], not “l'hockey”, and [[les | haricots]] (the beans), with no z sound. Most h's (as in [[hôtel]], [[hôpital]]) are silent and allow both.
- **Forgetting the CaReFuL letters:** [[avec]] is “a-vek”, not “a-vé”.

Even without liaison, French links words in speech: a pronounced final consonant runs into the next vowel. [[avec elle]] (with her) sounds like “a-vè-kel”, [[il a]] (he has) like “i-la”.

The result: spoken French sounds like one long stream of syllables. When you can't hear where a word starts, try moving the consonant: “lé-zami” is [[les amis]], “nou-zavons” is [[nous avons]].

- **Provinces and élision:** [[l'Ontario]], [[l'Alberta]], [[l'Île-du-Prince-Édouard]] use l'; [[le Québec]], [[le Manitoba]], [[la Saskatchewan]] don't, because they start with a consonant.
- **Hockey:** [[le hockey]] has an h that blocks élision. You'll hear it a lot in Canada!
- **Casual speech:** in relaxed conversation, especially in Québec, people often drop more sounds: [[je suis]] can sound like “j'suis” or even “chu”. This is informal: learn it for recognition only, and keep saying [[je suis]].

blocks.explain: Two élisions: ce → c', le → l'. hôtel has ô.
You hear z after nous and n after un, but you write the words separately.
[[d'accord]] = OK, agreed. The d is followed by an apostrophe.
The z sound (lé-z‿enfants) tells you it's [[les]]: plural.

models.label: Model reading
models.fr: Bonjour ! Ce sont mes amis, Karim et Amira. Ils ont deux enfants. Nous avons une heure. Un café ? D'accord ! Moi, j'ai un enfant.
models.en: Hello! These are my friends, Karim and Amira. They have two children. We have an hour. A coffee? OK! Me, I have one child.

blocks.prompt: Write 3 or 4 short sentences that use élision: at least one j', one l' and one d' or c'.
checklist: l' before a vowel or silent h
No « je ai » or « le ami »

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: J'ai un ami à Moncton. C'est l'ami de Lucie. Il est d'Ottawa. D'accord !
models.en: I have a friend in Moncton. He's Lucie's friend. He's from Ottawa. OK!

summary:
- Leave most final consonants silent, but say the **CaReFuL** ones: [[avec, bonjour, chef, hôtel]]
- Make liaisons: [[les amis, vous êtes, nous avons, un ami]], and never after [[et]]
- Use élision every time: [[j'ai, l'école, d'accord, c'est]]
